newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lights dim in Russian Far East as workers strike.
newsitem.headline: Lights dim in Russian Far East as workers strike.

text.p: Striking power workers blacked out parts of the Russian Far East on Monday, halving electricity output to protest that they had not been paid for months.
"We took a unanimous decision to strike until all salary debts are paid in full," strike leader Gennady Tkachuk told Russian television.
"Winter is coming. And if we don't get emergency help from the federal government...then winter is going to freeze the region," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying.
He said some homes and enterprises would be without electricity for 20 hours a day due to the strike, which started at 8 a.m. on Monday (2100 GMT on Sunday).

Some of the 16,000 power workers in the Pacific region have not been paid since April. The region has faced several bouts of industrial unrest this year -- miners went on strike in the summer to protest about unpaid wages.

Several hundred power workers demonstrated on Vladivostok's central square on Monday. "Truth, justice, legality," one banner said. The workers say they are owed 130 billion roubles ($24 million) in back wages.

On Monday they scorned an offer by regional governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko to resolve the energy crisis within two weeks if the strike was put on hold. Many blame the governor for a financial crisis at utility Dalenergo, which supplies the Pacific port of Vladivostok -- the largest city in the Russian Far East.
Tass quoted the workers as saying the governor had kept electricity rates low to help consumers, but this had brought the company to the brink of bankruptcy.

Local residents, already used to frequent power cuts, queued for candles and portable stoves. A small Korean-made camping stove costs 130,000 roubles ($25), or some 50,000 roubles more than it did a few weeks ago.

"It is very difficult to cook for a family on one ring," said Maria Azarova, an office worker going home on Monday night to make soup for five on a camping stove. "I am scared to use it and it is very expensive to pay for the gasoline."
The power company has promised to supply essential centres, including hospitals, bread factories and fire stations.
Other shops and offices are making do as best they can, trailing high-voltage cables from one building to the next.
"This is our way out," said reporter Viktor Serolyuk, whose newspaper Vladivostok has rigged up a cable from a nearby printing plant.
"Many companies are quietly finding links to buildings with electricity, although it is against fire safety rules."

Governor Nazdratenko has persuaded regional truck drivers to postpone their own planned strike, but on Friday several other maritime territory unions threatened to shut down firms across the region on October 10.
